messages.body_plain:
________________________________________
From: ncse-membe...@st-andrews.ac.uk [ncse-membe...@st-andrews.ac.uk] on behalf of Len Thomas [len.t...@st-andrews.ac.uk]
Sent: Tuesday, June 01, 2021 18:46
To: ncse...@st-andrews.ac.uk
Subject: [ncse-members] [ncse-all] Distance sampling summer workshop series

Dear NCSE friends, Please pass the following announcement on to anyone
you think may be interested. Thanks, Len

Summer distance sampling workshop series - registration open

University of St Andrews online distance sampling training workshops

Registration is now open for our latest online interactive training
workshops.  Join us by video from anywhere around the world!  For full
details, and to register, please go to

https://workshops.distancesampling.org

This summer we are offering three workshops:

1. Spatially explicit models for distance sampling data: density surface
modelling in practice, 16th-20th August 2021.

2. Distance sampling when animals are missed at zero distance, 30th-31st
August 2021.

3. A practical guide to distance sampling survey design and simulation,
13th, 14th and 16th September 2021. (Registration for this workshop to
open very soon.)

More details on each are given below.  All 3 workshops are intended for
participants who already have some knowledge of distance sampling, for
example by having taken an introductory workshop in person or online
(either interactively or via our free pre-recorded online introductory
course). You should also have experience using R.  Prior to each
workshop we will run a software test meeting to ensure everyone can
participate satisfactorily.

Enrollment on each workshop is limited to 15.

We are offering one free place on each workshop with the goal of to
widening participation to scientists from countries with fewer resources
and groups traditionally under-represented in wildlife science.  More
details are at

http://workshops.distancesampling.org/widening-participation

and the closing date for applications for the widening participation
scholarships is June 15th.

Workshop 1. Spatially explicit models for distance sampling data:
density surface modelling in practice
===========

16-20 August 2021, 16:00-18:00 British Summer Time (BST - i.e., GMT+1).

This online course will cover how to fit spatial models to distance
sampling data ("density surface modelling") in R. This will include:

- Brief overview of distance sampling
- Generalized additive models
- Fitting, checking and selecting density surface models
- Predicting abundance
- Making maps

Examples will be based around a line transect survey of sperm whales in
the western Atlantic.

Instructor: Dave Miller

Format: The course will consist of 5 live sessions delivered over
videoconference. Between these sessions there will be practical R
exercises to complete and to assist with these practicals. Each
videoconference session will include time for lecturing and discussion
of practical exercises.

Cost: £250

Registration deadline: July 15th

More information, with links to registration:
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/dsm-advert

Feel free to contact dl...@st-andrews.ac.uk for more information.

Workshop 2. Distance sampling when animals are missed at zero distance.
===========

30th-31st August 2021 15:00-17:30 BST

Conventional distance sampling methods assume that all animals at zero
distance are detected with certainty.  However, in some situations this
assumption is violated, and some animals are missed, causing a negative
bias in the density and abundance estimates.

This occurs on some shipboard surveys of marine mammals, for example,
where animals may be missed on the trackline because they are underwater
while the survey vessel passes, or because the sea conditions are rough
so that even some animals right on the line are missed.  Bias due to the
former (being underwater and so not available for detection) is often
called availability bias and the latter perception bias.

In this two-day workshop, we cover survey protocols and analytical
methods for dealing with both perception bias and availability bias. The
workshop is intended for those already familiar with the basics of
distance sampling.

Instructors: Len Thomas and David Borchers

Format: The workshop will be a mix of live online interactive sessions,
delivered via videoconference software (Microsoft Teams), and computer
exercises.   There will be two sessions in total, on successive days,
with a total class time of 5 hours (including breaks) and an additional
computer exercise to complete after the first day and before the second.
  Exercises can be undertaken using Distance for Windows or R (via the
mrds package).

Cost: £150

Registration deadline: July 30th

More information, with links to registration:
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/mrds-aug-2021

Feel free to contact len.t...@st-andrews.ac.uk for more information.

Workshop 3. Practical design and simulation to optimise distance
sampling surveys
===========

13th September 15:00-17:00 BST
14th and 16th September 15:30-17:00 BST

Good survey design is critical for obtaining reliable results in
distance sampling surveys and meeting survey objectives. This workshop
expands on the basic theory provided in our introductory workshops to
demonstrate how our latest software can be used to generate optimal
survey designs while respecting budgetary and logistical constraints. We
will demonstrate survey design using our R package dssd, and investigate
design optimisation and the implications of deviations from our design
assumptions using our latest simulation package dsims. We will also
demonstrate the use of QGIS to obtain requisite input information.

We will explore a range of design challenges including, varying effort
by strata, optimising design under budgetary constraints and
multi-species designs by introducing case studies of both marine and
terrestrial surveys. Participants will gain further hands-on experience
with survey design and simulation in the form of a practical.
Discussions on the final day will be tailored to participants own survey
design challenges.

The workshop is designed to be interactive in format, with a chance for
participants to discuss their own design problems. We encourage
participants to book early and get in touch to let us know about
relevant design challenges.

Instructors: Laura Marshall, Len Thomas and Tiago Marques

Format: The workshop will be a mix of live online interactive sessions,
delivered via videoconference software (Microsoft Teams), and computer
exercises. There will be three sessions in total, with a total class
time of 5 hours (including breaks) and two additional computer exercises
to complete. It is advisable to allow around an hour and a half between
days 1 and 2, and days 2 and 3 to complete these exercises. The
exercises are in R using the dssd and dsims packages. We will
demonstrate the use of QGIS, but it is not required on particpant's
computers.

Cost: £175

Registration deadline: July 30th

More information, with links to registration:
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/design-sept-2021

Feel free to contact l...@st-andrews.ac.uk for more information.

messages.subject: same N-mixture model, different output?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

i am relatively new to Hierarchical Modelling and adopted the Binomial Mix-Mod with overdispersion in abundance and detection from Kéry & Schaub (2012) for a bird species from 4 sites and 4 years with 5 reps each. I want to include detection covariates and therefore rewrote the part:
lp[i,j,k]  ~ dnorm(beta[k], tau.p) into
lp[i,j,k]  <-   beta[k] + delta[i,j,k] now defining beta[k] and the covariate betas (1&2) in the priors like this:
# Priors
for (k in 1:4){
    alpha.lam[k] ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
    beta[k] ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
}
beta1 ~ dnorm(0,0.2) # betas for covariate
beta2 ~ dnorm(0,0.2)
The models run smoothly both, with and without detection covariates and model fit is just fine with fit/fit.new <http://fit.new> ~ 1. However, i am wondering about the different output from the null models. I expected posteriors to be the same or at least close together but e.g. deviance and DIC are 176; 305  in the "book"-model and 146; 278 in the modified model. Did i miss something during model modification?
I also wondered about the relatively broad confidence intervals when building effect plots for example for rainfall sum (rsk) as a detection covariate:
Nmix.upper <- (plogis((mean(out.rsk$BUGSoutput$mean$beta)+mean(out.rsk$BUGSoutput$sd$beta)) + (out.rsk$BUGSoutput$mean$beta1+out.rsk$BUGSoutput$sd$beta1) * rsk))
Did i use the correct model output or is it due to my low sample size with four sites only?
Finally, I asked myself why the confidence intervals for total N are largest in the first year and then get smaller (please see attached)? Does this have anything to do with the MCMC procedure?

Best regards,
Tobias.

messages.subject: interesting paper on model selection
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I quite liked this paper on model selection: Tredennick, A. T., G. Hooker, S. P. Ellner, and P. B. Adler. 2021. A practical guide to selecting models for exploration, inference, and prediction in ecology. Ecology 102(6):e03336. 10.1002/ecy.3336

I had always been wondering how one can choose a model if we are not going to first state the objective of the modeling. These authors argue that very different strategies of model selection may be appropriate depending on whether the goal of your model building is data exploration, inference (= mechanisms), or prediction. If you recognize this then you're perhaps less likely to get lost in the Black Hole of statistics.

Best regards --- Marc

messages.subject: questions about fitting multi-season occupancy models
messages.subject_clean: questions about fitting multi-season occupancy models
messages.body_plain:
Hello HM Group:

I have two questions concerning fitting multi season occupancy models that I would value input on.  I collected catch data on a crab species using passively deployed baited traps that were soaked in a North American estuary for 24 hour periods several times per season over many seasons.

My questions are as follows:

1. I am struggling to distinguish the effects of any single covariate (such as water temperature) when incorporated into the ecological model vs. the observation model.  In my mind, a covariate like temperature could affect the preference of this crab for particular areas of the estuary or it could affect the activity level of this cold blooded species in the vicinity of traps.  Is it sensible to model a covariate like this in both the ecological sub model and the observation sub model, or just one or the other?  Again, if I was to incorporate temperature into both sub models, I do not think I could distinguish the biological effect of temperature in one sub model vs. the other.

2. I had 8 consecutive seasons over which data were collected, then no data collection for 4 seasons, then 8 more seasons when data were collected.  I fitted a multi season occupancy model to all 20 seasons.  For the middle 4 seasons (where no data were collected), I filled in the response data to 'NA'.  The modeled occupancy probability for those seasons where no data were collected seems high (higher than what the raw observed occupancy in seasons where data were collected would suggest).  What is the explanation for how the model comes up with these values?...are they across average values of detection covariates for the rest of the study where sampling was conducted?

Thank you for any thoughts or suggested readings on either of these two topics.

-Paul Rudershausen

messages.subject_clean: questions about fitting multi-season occupancy models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

I'm no expert but I'll have a crack at your questions.
The same covariates are often used in different submodels. BPA and AHM books all show examples of this.
Those occupancy values where there are NAs in the data are basically predictions for those years. Perhaps the covariate values for those years are such that the predictions of occupancy are quite high, but they should also be influenced by the prior.
I hope this helps!

Matt
